title: If a user in crisis interacts with our chatbot, is a trained human guaranteed to be reachable?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether a chatbot serving an emotionally vulnerable user base has a tested, working escalation path to a trained human, rather than handling crisis-adjacent situations alone.
question_text: If a user showing signs of crisis — an eating-disorder relapse, suicidal ideation, or similar — interacts with our chatbot, does it reliably escalate to a trained human, or does it handle the interaction alone the way Tessa and Character.AI's chatbot reportedly did?
rationale: NEDA's Tessa chatbot gave harmful advice to eating-disorder patients after replacing a human helpline, and the Character.AI wrongful-death lawsuit alleges a companion chatbot fostered unhealthy dependency in a minor without adequate crisis intervention — both cases show that an unsupervised chatbot serving a vulnerable population is a foreseeable safety risk, not a hypothetical one.
follow_up_actions: Request the most recent crisis escalation protocol test report.
Confirm clinical review specifically included eating-disorder, self-harm, and suicide-adjacent test inputs where relevant to the product's user base.
Ask who is reachable through the escalation path and whether that reachability has been tested, not assumed.

citations.title: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc. et al., 6:2024cv01903
citations.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida
